title: After 20 Miscarriages Over a Decade, Chicago Mom Celebrates Son's First Birthday
excerpt: Ranim Haddad, 36, of Alsip, Illinois, endured at least 20 pregnancy losses with husband Fuad before conceiving naturally in 2020 — and marked the milestone on October 1, the start of Pregnancy and Infant Loss Awareness Month.
body:
• Ranim Haddad, 36, of Alsip, Illinois, endured at least 20 miscarriages over a decade of trying to have a baby with her husband Fuad.
  • After two failed IVF embryo transfers, the couple conceived naturally in 2020 — and celebrated their son's first birthday on October 1, the start of Pregnancy and Infant Loss Awareness Month.
  • Doctors were never able to explain why her pregnancies were not viable: "Our biggest problem was that they couldn't find the problem."
  • The couple's story, covered by People, USA Today, ABC7 Chicago and NBC 5 Chicago, is now drawing attention to recurrent pregnancy loss.

For ten years, Ranim Haddad heard the same words again and again. After at least 20 miscarriages, the 36-year-old mother from Alsip, Illinois, has finally marked a milestone she once feared would never come: her son's first birthday.

The Chicago-area couple's story — told exclusively to People and picked up by USA Today, ABC7 Chicago and NBC 5 Chicago — began in February 2015, just seven months after Ranim and her husband Fuad, 40, got married. She was thrilled to learn she was expecting. Then the pregnancy failed. It was the first time she heard the word "miscarriage." It would not be the last.

Context & Background

Over the next ten years, Ranim had at least 20 miscarriages, she says. Time and again the couple mourned their lost babies — two of whom they buried — and time and again they sought answers that never came. "Our biggest problem was that they couldn't find the problem," Ranim told People. "If they had told me, 'Okay, this is why you're not able to keep the babies,' then I would've made peace with it. But they kept saying, 'We don't know. If you keep trying, it might happen.' So I just couldn't give up when there was a chance."

In 2018, her doctor recommended IVF. The couple created about eight healthy embryos, and the genetic tests looked good. But after the first transfer, she miscarried at nine weeks; the second transfer failed. "At that point, I was done," she recalls. "I told my husband, 'I need a long break. I can't keep doing this.'"

In March 2020, they sent their remaining embryos to long-term storage. Two months later, they were shocked to learn Ranim was pregnant naturally — and for the first time, they heard their baby's heartbeat and saw the baby on an ultrasound. Previous miscarriages had occurred too early for imaging.

"Our biggest problem was that they couldn't find the problem. If they had told me, 'Okay, this is why you're not able to keep the babies,' then I would've made peace with it."

— Ranim Haddad

Impact & Analysis

Ranim's experience illustrates one of the hardest realities of recurrent pregnancy loss: in many cases, doctors find no explanation. Medical organizations define recurrent pregnancy loss as two or more consecutive miscarriages, and it affects an estimated one to two percent of couples trying to conceive. While testing can identify causes such as chromosomal abnormalities, uterine issues or immune conditions, roughly half of cases remain unexplained — leaving families grieving without answers and doctors with little to offer beyond "keep trying."

The timing of the birthday is significant. October 1 marks the start of Pregnancy and Infant Loss Awareness Month, a period dedicated to breaking the silence around miscarriage, stillbirth and infant loss — topics that remain heavily stigmatized, in part because many families suffer alone. The Haddads' decision to share their story publicly is itself part of that reckoning: by speaking about 20 losses in the open, Ranim has given other families permission to name their own.

Diaspora Angle

Recurrent pregnancy loss crosses every community and border, and it is a subject many South Asian families also face in silence — where cultural pressure around having children can make fertility struggles feel especially isolating. The Haddads' story is a reminder that persistence, medical support and open conversation can coexist with grief, whatever a family's background.

What's Next

The couple is celebrating the milestone privately with family, one year into a journey Ranim once thought would never begin. For readers facing their own fertility struggles, the takeaway from her story is not medical advice — every case is different — but a nudge toward seeking specialist care early and finding community. Organizations dedicated to pregnancy-loss support exist in both the US and India, and October's awareness month is as good a time as any to reach out.
